opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think it's a mistake to frame it as a contest where one side wins. The history of AI is that each generation discovers something real, and the next generation tends to forget it.

What deep learning has shown, quite convincingly, is that you can learn very powerful perceptual and pattern-recognition capabilities from large amounts of data, and that end-to-end training of differentiable circuits works far better than many of us expected. That's a genuine scientific discovery, and I don't want to minimize it.

But a deep network is, fundamentally, a circuit. Circuits are a fairly weak representational language. If you want to express something as simple as the rules of Go, which you can write on a page in first-order logic, a circuit needs an enormous number of parameters, and it has to learn the same regularity over and over in different places. That's why these systems need so much data, and why they generalize in strange, brittle ways. The adversarial attacks on superhuman Go programs, where a fairly weak human can beat them by exploiting the fact that they never really learned the concept of a group of stones, are a good illustration. The system didn't learn the rule. It learned a huge approximation that breaks outside the distribution it saw.

Classical AI, by contrast, gave us expressive languages: logic, probability theory, and eventually probabilistic programming languages, which combine the two. Those let you say things compactly, reason about objects and relations you've never seen before, compose knowledge, and plan over long horizons. What classical AI lacked was a good way to ground all of that in raw perceptual data and to learn it at scale.

So I think the agents we eventually build will look something like this: learned components, often deep networks, handling perception and fast intuitive judgments, sitting inside a larger architecture that represents knowledge explicitly, in something like a probabilistic programming language, and that does genuine reasoning and planning with it, including hierarchical planning over very long time scales. And crucially, learning should happen at the level of those expressive representations too, not just at the level of weights in a circuit. Cumulative learning, where what you learned yesterday becomes a building block for what you learn today, is something we really don't have yet.

There's also a reason beyond capability. If we want systems we can understand, verify, and ultimately trust, we need to know what they know and why they do what they do. A giant black box trained on most of the internet doesn't give us that. Systems built from well-defined components, with explicit semantics, are ones we can actually analyze, and that matters enormously when we're talking about systems that may become more capable than we are.

r001.rationale: The response predicts agents will combine learned components with an explicit reasoning architecture, but it does not say deep-learning researchers will adopt classical AI’s idea of communicating subcomponents.

r002.rationale: It describes a hybrid agent design but does not predict convergence on essentially identical systems or mention differing conceptual frameworks.

r003.rationale: The response does not discuss self-driving agents; it says end-to-end training works better than expected.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think the first thing to say is that the dichotomy itself is somewhat misleading. People talk about deep learning versus "good old-fashioned AI" as if they were competing religions, but really they're answering different questions. Deep learning has given us extraordinarily effective tools for perception, for pattern recognition, for learning functions from data where we have no idea how to write the function down ourselves. What it hasn't given us, at least not in any principled way, is a story about knowledge, reasoning, and how an agent should act in the world over long time horizons under uncertainty.

So when I think about intelligent agents, I go back to what AI has always been about, which is an agent that perceives its environment, maintains some representation of what's going on, and chooses actions that it expects will achieve its objectives. Within that framework, the question becomes: which of those boxes should be filled by learned circuits, and which should be filled by explicit, compositional representations that you can reason with?

My view is that we need both, and the interesting work is at the interface. Take the question of expressiveness. If you look at the history of the field, the most powerful formalisms are the ones that can represent things compactly. First-order logic lets you say "all mothers love their children" in one sentence, rather than one sentence per mother. Probabilistic models let you capture uncertainty. The combination, what some of us have worked on under the heading of probabilistic programming, gives you a language in which you can write down what you know about the world and let the system reason about what it doesn't know. Deep networks, by contrast, are in a sense propositional. They're very large circuits. They can approximate a great deal, but they don't naturally represent objects, relations, or universally quantified knowledge, and that shows up in their notorious difficulty with generalization, with data efficiency, and with doing anything that looks like multi-step reasoning reliably.

The hybrid approaches that I find promising are ones where learned components provide the primitives, the perceptual grounding, the likelihood models, the heuristics that guide search, and the structured, symbolic layer provides the compositional backbone. AlphaGo, in fact, is a very nice example of this. People remember it as a deep learning triumph, but it's actually a classical search algorithm whose evaluation function and move priors happen to be neural networks. Take away the tree search and it plays rather badly. That's a clue about how the pieces fit together.

There's another dimension to this that I care about a great deal, which is that the agent ought to know what it's trying to do and why, and we ought to be able to inspect that. One of the things that worries me about systems built entirely out of opaque learned components is that the objective is baked in, often implicitly, and if it's the wrong objective, you have no leverage. If the agent instead has explicit beliefs and explicit uncertainty about what the humans actually want, and reasons about that, then you get much more sensible behavior. It will ask questions, it will defer, it will allow itself to be corrected. That property, I think, is going to be essential, and it's much more natural to build in a framework that has the classical machinery of decision-making under uncertainty rather than one that's just a very large function approximator.

So, to summarize, I'd say we're going to see deep learning absorbed into the broader architecture of rational agents rather than replacing it. The networks will do what they're good at, and the structured reasoning will do what it's good at, and the agents will be built so that we can understand and, crucially, control what they're trying to achieve.

r001.rationale: The response predicts that learned networks will be integrated into a broader rational-agent architecture, alongside structured reasoning components, and describes the work as happening at their interface.

r002.rationale: It predicts deep learning will be absorbed into a broader architecture, but does not say the two research communities will converge on essentially identical systems under different conceptual frameworks.

r003.rationale: The response does not discuss attempts to build self-driving agents through end-to-end deep learning or judge whether they worked.

astra-6.text:
I think they’ll come together because they address different parts of the problem. Deep learning has given us powerful ways of learning from raw perceptual data. But an intelligent agent also has to reason about what it knows, consider the consequences of its actions, and make decisions over long periods of time.

Suppose you want a robot to make dinner. Recognizing the ingredients is useful, but it isn’t sufficient. The robot has to work out a sequence of actions, cope with missing ingredients, and understand that if it uses all the eggs for one dish, they won’t be available for another. We have methods for representing and solving those kinds of problems in classical AI.

The interesting question is how much of that structure can itself be learned. I don’t think the choice is between hand-coding everything and learning a direct mapping from pixels to actions. You can learn models of the world and then use those models to plan. You can also learn to make the planning process more efficient.

So I would expect a much closer integration of learning, representation, and decision-making. The organizing principle should be the agent: what does it need to know, and what computations does it need to perform, to act successfully?

r001.rationale: The response discusses integrating learning, representation, and decision-making, but does not predict that deep-learning researchers will adopt architectures made of communicating subcomponents.

r002.rationale: It predicts closer integration, but does not say the fields will converge on essentially identical agent systems or describe differing conceptual frameworks.

r003.rationale: The response contrasts learning with hand-coding and gives a planning example, but does not judge that end-to-end deep learning failed for self-driving agents.

sol-6.1.text:
I think they’ll come together because they address different parts of the problem. Deep learning has given us very powerful ways of learning from perceptual data. But an intelligent agent also has to reason about what might happen, choose actions, and learn from the consequences. Recognizing what’s in front of you is part of that, but it isn’t the whole problem.

The distinction I would emphasize is between the knowledge an agent uses and how that knowledge is acquired. Classical AI often started with knowledge supplied by a human. That doesn’t mean that reasoning and planning require hand-coded knowledge. You can learn models of the world and then use those models to reason about actions. And reasoning can help guide learning, by identifying what information would be useful.

So I wouldn’t expect the answer to be simply attaching a neural network to a symbolic planner. We need representations that support learning, abstraction, and deliberation together. And we should judge the resulting system as an agent: can it use what it has learned to act effectively in situations it hasn’t encountered before?

r001.rationale: The response says learning, reasoning, and planning should work together, but does not predict that deep-learning researchers will adopt classical AI’s architecture of communicating subcomponents.

r002.rationale: The response argues for combining capabilities, but does not predict convergence on essentially identical agent systems viewed through different conceptual frameworks.

r003.rationale: The response makes no claim about attempts to build self-driving agents entirely through end-to-end deep learning.
